extracted.intended_audience: political theorists, legislators, and constitutional designers interested in principles for structuring governments
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and judging constitutional arrangements (term limits, election frequency, separation of powers, minority protections, accountability mechanisms) for their practical effects on liberty, corruption, and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to enforced rotation / term limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental law that no man shall serve in the sovereign assembly more than one year, or two or three years, or one in three, &c., is a violation of the rights of mankind; it is an abridgment of the rights both of electors and candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forced rotation deprives people of choosing the ablest and best men and compels the removal of experienced, meritorious officeholders; even if the law were obeyed, incumbents would nominate successors and continue governing in effect. Term limits therefore can be contrary to the rights of electors and may multiply factions rather than remove them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks on power more important than mere limitation of duration
rubrics_metrics.description: It was powers being undefined, unlimited by law, and unchecked that made bodies (e.g., the Roman senate) factious, not merely the prolongation of power in particular persons or families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cause of faction is unchecked authority; therefore constitutional design should focus on defining and limiting powers and providing countervailing constitutional checks rather than relying on rotation or short terms alone to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of frequent elections as remedy for self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession of powers and persons by frequent elections will not lessen selfish passions in any case; nor will the apprehension of an approaching election restrain those in power from indulgence if they have the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent elections (annual elections of governors, senators, representatives) provide succession but do not by themselves cure self-interest, bribery, or corruption; other institutional restraints are necessary to control the private avidity of officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws as the foundation of liberty and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Those laws which alone can secure equity between all and everyone are the foundation of liberty and the fountain of equity; laws should be right reason derived from the Divinity, commanding honesty and forbidding iniquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should build on a rule-of-law conception where laws act as 'silent magistrates' rather than leaving liberty to the uncertain virtue of rulers or majorities; legal foundations rooted in moral principles secure impartiality and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for mixed government with separated powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed government (separate branches with mutual checks) is preferable to a single sovereign assembly annually elected, which is particularly well calculated to facilitate gratification of self-love and private interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed constitutions allow ministers and executives to be held responsible (impeachment, trial by senate, independent judges), provide internal checks (senate, governor, house restraining each other), and reduce the ease with which a single assembly can become oligarchic or corrupt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards for minority rights
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no possible way of defending the minority in a single sovereign assembly except by giving the minority a negative (veto), otherwise the majority will instantly oppress the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While protecting minorities is essential, unanimity or absolute veto mechanisms (liberum veto) are also dangerous; constitutional design must provide effective minority safeguards without producing paralysis or external vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for political accountability and redress
rubrics_metrics.description: In a mixed government, ministers of the executive are responsible for the exercise of power and may, by impeachment, be made responsible before a senate, tried, condemned, and punished by independent judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clear accountability channels (impeachment, trials before independent bodies) so that abuses of executive power can be punished. Contrast this with a single assembly where members are typically responsible only to their personal constituents who may applaud abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of patronage, bribery, and capture of public institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections tend to make every passion and prejudice of every voter available to flattery, menace, trick, bribe; offices, contracts, pensions, shares in loans and contracts are distributed among friends, enabling the drawing in of instruments and worming out of opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should limit opportunities for patronage and the distribution of public emoluments as political rewards (controls on appointments, public contracting rules, independent appointment processes, transparent finance) because capture of the judiciary, press, professions, and cultural institutions follows from unrestrained patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assemblies can rapidly become oligarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereignty in one assembly, successively chosen by the people, is perhaps an aristocracy as despotical as a Roman senate and becomes an oligarchy even sooner than a hereditary aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary that recurring elections can entrench a small number of influential actors (by art, address, opulence, birth, connections) who perpetuate themselves across elections; institutional countermeasures are required to prevent formation of an entrenched oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimity requirements (liberum veto) are politically ruinous
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberum veto — requiring unanimity — allows one bribed or foolish member to prevent measures essential to defense, safety, and existence of the nation; it has produced humiliation and partitions (example: Poland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constitutional rules that mandate unanimity for ordinary decision-making; seek balanced checks rather than unanimity, which invites foreign intrigue and paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent judiciary as interpreter and safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are the interpreters of the law; they are crucial servants of the law and liberty, and must be independent so that the laws function as silent magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure judicial independence from legislative/executive capture (appointment safeguards, tenure protections) so courts can check abuses and maintain the rule of law amidst political competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent continuation of power via corruption to avoid rebellion
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation of power will be accomplished by corruption, which is worse than continuation by birth; if corruption cannot effect the continuation, sedition and rebellion will be recurred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must reduce avenues for corrupt entrenchment of power, since corruption breeds deeper instability and can provoke violent backlash when elites are frustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs between hereditary stability and frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases first magistrates and senators might be better made hereditary than suffer annual fraud and violence; hereditary descent may become less evil than annual fraud if elections are universally debauched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize tradeoffs: stability and moral-preserving mechanisms in hereditary or long-tenure designs versus the risks of corrupt, violent, or fraudulent frequent elections. Mechanisms like conventions can sometimes mitigate worst outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The majority can itself be a faction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the majority are partial in their own favour and refuse equality to the minority, they are a faction; every popular assembly that votes divides into majority and minority, and the majority acting unjustly is a faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the majority not as intrinsically benign — design checks (institutional balances, protections for minority rights, restraint mechanisms) because majorities can pursue private interests and tyrannize minorities.
